results.summary: Glyph Mode HD renders a Matrix-style digital rain animation to a VGA display, with glyphs falling from the top and intermittently changing. Eight input pins select one of eight palettes, palette mixing, pause, an alternative pattern, and one of four display timing modes. It requires the TinyVGA PMOD and a clock matched to the selected mode, with 25.175 MHz for standard VGA and 74.25 MHz for 720p or 1080p30. The design was tested on a Basys 3 with a 4K monitor through a VGA-to-HDMI converter, and 1080p60 was not achievable so FHD at 30 FPS was chosen.

OIIA-goose displays a rotating goose demoscene with four selectable backgrounds and classic OIIA music. Two input pins choose the background and two choose the spin mode, while an audio PWM output carries the music and RGB222 VGA outputs drive a display. It needs the TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, and the goose sprite data must be generated with the provided Python extraction script. The documentation is brief and does not describe the audio generation or the exact background behavior in detail.

Goose Game is a Chrome Dino-style endless runner in which a goose jumps over scrolling University of Waterloo emblem obstacles. It outputs RGB222 VGA at 640x480 and 60 Hz, with a button input for jumping and a reset input. It requires the TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor plus a push button. The documentation is short and gives no detail on scoring, difficulty, or verification.

GrammarTile is a byte-level NFA plus bounded pushdown automaton accelerator with a baked JSON grammar that classifies streamed bytes against a grammar. A host loads a PDA state, advances bytes one at a time over SPI or an 8-bit parallel fast path, and reads back an accept bit, with checkpoint and restore commands to reuse a starting state. Status pins expose accept, ready, error, and four NFA state bits, and the design is verified with a self-checking cocotb test over a JSON corpus. It targets the Tiny Tapeout demo board with RP2040 SPI, or an optional DIP switch and button harness for parallel mode.

HSXO wraps a high-speed crystal oscillator IP block from Chipalooza 2024 into the Tiny Tapeout analog template. It forms a Pierce oscillator when a passive crystal is bridged between XIN and XOUT with load capacitors to ground, and it needs a 1 uA bias current on IBIAS plus ENA high and STDBY low. A clock appears on DOUT after a start-up delay, and XIN and XOUT can be probed while accounting for probe loading. The block could theoretically support 4 to 16 MHz crystals, but the higher end needs shorter traces than the demo board provides.

Speck-V SoC is a TinyQV RISC-V system on chip with custom ISA extensions for the SPECK-ARX lightweight block cipher. It exposes UART, SPI, QSPI flash and PSRAM interfaces, GPIO, interrupts, and a debug UART, matching the QSPI Flash/PSRAM and SPI Pmod pinouts. It runs at 64 MHz and is intended as a microcontroller-class platform for lightweight cryptography workloads. The documentation provided here is limited to the title, pin names, and pinout match, so the custom instruction details and test results are not described.

CFAR Radar Detector is a low-area cell-averaging constant false alarm rate accelerator that estimates background noise from a sliding window of training cells around a cell under test. Radar amplitude samples arrive on the 8-bit input bus, and a detection is asserted when the cell under test exceeds twice the averaged noise, with a buzzer alert output. It is fully digital and needs no external hardware, though outputs could drive a buzzer, LED, or radar front end. It is verified in Icarus Verilog with a testbench and an example input sequence containing a strong reflection.

Mrudul and Wahhaj Demoscene F2025 renders a Bad Time Sans fight scene in which a goose plays Sans and a University of Waterloo heart appears. Four speed bits and a direction pin control the animation, and RGB222 VGA outputs drive a display. It requires the TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. The documentation is essentially absent beyond the title and pin names, so the scene contents and behavior are only inferred.

Analog Readout Circuit measures capacitors by charging them with selectable current sources and timing the result with a counter. Switches select small, medium, or large capacitor ranges, pulse delay pins control small-signal timing, and current source control pins select transistor lengths, with the analog inputs connected to a capacitor and a comparator reference voltage. The 8-bit counter result appears on the digital outputs and the design runs from a 1 to 20 MHz clock with a reset button. It needs a button, a voltage source, and a microcontroller for control, and the documentation is a pin-by-pin usage guide rather than a full description.

UART Positioning PWM Interface receives UART commands and generates a 20 ms servo control frame with pulse widths from about 1.0 ms to 2.0 ms. Commands select minimum, center, maximum, digit presets, or sweep mode, and dedicated pins can force the three preset positions directly. Status outputs report command acknowledgement, preset code, failsafe activation, and sweep mode, and the design returns to center after inactivity. It needs a 25 MHz clock, a USB-to-UART adapter or microcontroller TX line, and an externally powered hobby servo or a logic analyzer, and it includes a cocotb regression.
